content: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP) is defined as a sudden, unexpected death in individuals with epilepsy that is not caused by trauma, drowning, or prolonged seizures (status epilepticus) and where postmortem examination does not reveal a structural or toxicological cause. The incidence of SUDEP is estimated to be 1 to 2 cases per 1000 patient-years, making it the leading cause of epilepsy-related mortality. Risk factors for SUDEP include the presence and frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS), male sex, early onset of epilepsy, longer duration of epilepsy, and the use of multiple antiepileptic drugs (polytherapy). Although the exact mechanisms underlying SUDEP remain unclear, dysfunction in cardiac, respiratory, and brainstem systems triggered by GTCS is thought to play a significant role. Approximately 70% of individuals with epilepsy can achieve complete seizure control with appropriately selected antiepileptic drug therapy. However, about one-third of patients remain drug-resistant despite polytherapy, leaving them at continued risk for SUDEP, depression, and diminished quality of life. Preventative strategies for SUDEP focus on reducing the occurrence of GTCS through timely presurgical evaluations for individuals with lesional epilepsy, lifestyle modifications, and the use of seizure-monitoring devices. Other measures include nocturnal supervision and safety pillows to prevent airway obstruction, physical stimulation to counteract central hypoventilation, and pharmacological interventions such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) to enhance serotonergic regulation of respiration. Additional strategies aim to mitigate brain and brainstem depression caused by adenosine and endogenous opioids. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions in preventing SUDEP by synthesizing evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cohort studies, and case-control studies. The search for relevant studies included multiple databases and registries, with no language restrictions, and spanned from 1823 to 2019. Grey literature and unpublished materials were also considered. The review included randomized and non-randomized studies that assessed interventions such as early versus delayed presurgical evaluation, educational programs, seizure-monitoring devices, safety pillows, nocturnal supervision, SSRIs, opiate antagonists, and adenosine antagonists. From an initial pool of 1277 records, 33 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 29 studies were excluded for reasons such as not evaluating SUDEP prevention interventions, being review articles, or lacking control groups. Ultimately, one cohort study and three case-control studies were included, though all were deemed to have a serious to critical risk of bias. The 6-month prospective cohort study investigated the impact of providing SUDEP-related information on medication adherence, quality of life, and levels of anxiety and depression. However, the study was too short to observe any deaths, and no significant effects were found on the measured outcomes. Two case-control studies suggested that nocturnal supervision may have a protective effect against SUDEP. One study, involving 154 SUDEP cases and 616 controls, reported an unadjusted odds ratio (OR) of 0.34 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.53; P < 0.0001), indicating a significant protective effect independent of seizure control. Another study, with 48 SUDEP cases and 220 controls, reported an unadjusted OR of 0.08 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.27; P < 0.0001). However, due to significant heterogeneity, the results could not be pooled for meta-analysis. A third case-control study, conducted in residential care centers where patients already received physical checks more than 15 minutes apart during the night, did not find additional protective effects from more frequent checks, listening devices, dormitory settings, or bed sensors. However, the study noted that centers with lower levels of supervision had higher incidences of SUDEP. None of the case-control studies reported on quality of life or anxiety and depression outcomes. In conclusion, the evidence supporting nocturnal supervision as a protective measure against SUDEP is limited and of very low certainty. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of other interventions, such as seizure detection devices, safety pillows, SSRIs, early surgical evaluation, educational programs, and pharmacological agents like opiate and adenosine antagonists, in reducing the risk of SUDEP in individuals with epilepsy.
